modelResponse.episodeSummary: Eleanor R. Vance, Junctional Rhythm, warning, hemodynamically stable
keyECGEvidence: morphology: Narrow QRS, scooped ST, slow regular rhythm despite AFib
preEventNote: Known AFib now with slow REGULAR response — suggests AV junctional takeover
modelResponse.mechanism: Increased vagal tone and direct AV nodal inhibition by digoxin leading to AV block and escape rhythm from the AV junction.
contributingFactors: Hypokalemia (K 5.6 mmol/L HIGH - note: this is hyperkalemia, but digoxin toxicity can cause both hypo- and hyperkalemia, and hyperkalemia can worsen AV block)
Dehydration / Decreased urine output (impaired digoxin clearance)

rejectedAlternatives.why: Patient has known AFib, and the rhythm is regular, not sinus bradycardia or sinus arrest. The ECG morphology and clinical context strongly point to digoxin effect.
While possible given age, the acute onset, associated symptoms (nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance), and markedly elevated digoxin level make toxicity the most likely cause.
While K is HIGH (5.6 mmol/L), the ECG does not show classic hyperkalemia changes (peaked T waves, widened QRS). The scooped ST segments and clinical picture are more consistent with digoxin toxicity.

recommendedActions: Administer Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digibind/DigiFab) per protocol given TOXIC level (3.8 ng/mL) and symptomatic bradycardia
Monitor ECG continuously for changes in rhythm or conduction
Consider temporary pacing if bradycardia becomes hemodynamically unstable or refractory to Digibind
Withhold other AV nodal blocking agents if any are present
uncertainty: Exact contribution of hyperkalemia to bradycardia is unclear without more specific ECG findings.
Severity of dehydration is not fully quantified.
